summary: Gives guidelines for using IPv6 transition mechanisms during IPv6 deployment, helping operators choose among the many deployment models. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6180 compares ways to introduce IPv6 while some networks and applications still use IPv4. It recommends choosing a model that keeps services working and can be operated and changed over time.

subtitle: Guidance on choosing among four IPv6 deployment models and their transition mechanisms.

tldr.problem: Network operators need to deploy IPv6 while supporting IPv4 systems and services, and the available transition models have different requirements and trade-offs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives principles for selecting a model and discusses native dual stack, tunnels across IPv4 networks, an IPv6-only provider core, and IPv6-only domains with translation.
tldr.outcome: The document recommends enabling IPv6 and prioritizing native dual stack or tunneling where they fit. It is Informational guidance, and the operator must choose for its own network.

today: RFC 6180 is an Informational RFC published in May 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; its IPv4 address figures and deployment observations describe the period covered by the text.

sections.title: Why Operators Need Transition Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC describes IPv4 address exhaustion as a reason to deploy IPv6 and says that IPv6 deployment takes planning, resources, and expertise. Network managers face several deployment models and transition tools that were designed for different situations.

The document offers guidance for common cases, not every possible network. It says managers remain responsible for choosing a solution and planning a step-wise transition for their own environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need more address space, but they cannot all change networks in the same way. This document compares common approaches and leaves the final choice to each network manager.

sections.title: Principles for Choosing a Model
sections.content:
The long-term goal is native IPv6 across networks, which would remove the need for transitional tunnels and translation and eventually remove the need for IPv4. Until then, IPv4-only systems and services must still be considered in most networks.

The RFC prioritizes working communication over small performance gains. It favors incremental deployment, simple and scalable designs, tools that can be removed after coexistence, and systems that operators can maintain and diagnose. Deployment is normally step-wise; for example, IPv6 connectivity should be established and tested before IPv6 addresses are placed in DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: Choose a plan that keeps communication working and can be introduced in stages. A temporary transition tool should be removable when it is no longer needed.

sections.title: Native Dual Stack and Tunnels
sections.content:
Native dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 in the existing network. The RFC recommends it for most networks because it supports end-to-end choice of protocol and avoids tunnel configuration and tunnel MTU complications. Actual IPv6 traffic still depends on peers, applications, and naming services supporting IPv6; unreliable IPv6 paths can also delay some applications from switching to IPv4.

When native IPv6 is unavailable across part of a path, a tunnel can carry IPv6 across IPv4. Tunnels decouple addressing inside and outside the tunnel, but add configuration and path-MTU considerations. The RFC recommends tunneling when a network must cross an IPv4 segment and native connectivity cannot be established.
sections.plainLanguage: Running both IP versions in the same network is the preferred approach for most cases. If an IPv4-only segment blocks IPv6, a tunnel can carry IPv6 through that segment.

sections.title: An IPv6-Only Core with IPv4 Service
sections.content:
A service provider may run IPv6 in its core and carry IPv4 traffic through that network. The RFC identifies IPv4 address shortages, the need to reach address-sharing equipment, and a desire to operate one protocol in the core as reasons for this model.

It recommends Dual Stack Lite for this scenario. Dual Stack Lite carries IPv4 over IPv6 while allowing the provider network to move toward IPv6. The model can also make IPv6 connectivity available to end users over the provider's IPv6 network.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider can use IPv6 in its internal network while still carrying customers' IPv4 traffic. Dual Stack Lite is the tool this RFC recommends for that model.

sections.title: IPv4 and IPv6-Only Domains
sections.content:
An IPv6-only network may need to communicate with IPv4-only hosts or services. The RFC discusses application proxies and relays, as well as network-layer IPv4/IPv6 translation. A small set of systems can use IPv4-mapped addresses for stateless interoperation; many client systems can instead reach IPv4 servers through stateful translation.

Translation has limits. Shared IPv4 addresses can retain issues similar to IPv4 NAT, and IPv4 address literals inside application content may not work for an IPv6-only host. The RFC prefers proxies or relays at the application layer to application-layer gateways in translators. It describes NAT-PT as problematic and points to RFC 4966.
sections.plainLanguage: Translation can connect an IPv6-only network to IPv4 services, but some applications still depend on IPv4 details. Proxies, relays, or dual stack may be better when those details cause problems.

sections.title: Recommendations and Security
sections.content:
The RFC's central recommendation is to deploy IPv6. It recommends all four models, with native dual stack and tunneling taking priority where they apply. The best choice depends on existing equipment, the need to connect IPv4-only systems, and the degree of control the operator has over devices and services.

IPv4 and IPv6 face similar security threats, but network components still need appropriate IPv6 security capabilities, including firewall support. The RFC says it does not change the security properties of the specific transition tools; their defining documents discuss those issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The main advice is to begin IPv6 deployment using a model that fits the network. Operators must also make sure their monitoring, firewalls, and other security tools handle IPv6 traffic.
